hook.question: A printer has 20 jobs waiting. When the first one finishes, who prints next, and how does the computer keep the line without sliding all the other jobs forward?
paragraphs: Jobs must print in the order they arrived. Store them in a row of boxes and the first job sits in box 0. When it finishes, the obvious fix is to slide jobs 2 to 20 one box to the left: 19 moves for every page that prints.
That is a lot of shuffling just to forget one job. What if every job stayed exactly where it is, and only something small changed?
hook.aha: Move the markers, not the jobs. front remembers which box holds the next job to print, and back remembers where the next newcomer goes. Both only move forward, and after the last box they wrap round to box 0 to reuse the boxes that finished jobs left behind. Each step is one small change, however long the line is.

metaphor: A ticket counter calls tickets in the order people joined the line: newcomers go to the back, the front is served next, and nobody walks forward when someone leaves.
Now picture a sushi belt with 6 spots that loops back on itself. After spot 5 comes spot 0 again, so a spot you just emptied is the next one a new plate can use. That belt is a circular buffer.
mentalModel.click: Nobody in the line moves, only two markers do: front says who is served next, back says where the newcomer goes, and both wrap from the last slot to slot 0.

glossary.definition: Join the line: put a new item at the back.
Serve the line: remove and return the item at the front.
The oldest item, the next one to leave. Also called the head.
The newest item, the last to arrive. Also called the tail or rear.
First in, first out. Items leave in exactly the order they arrived.
A fixed array treated as a loop: front and back move forward with % capacity, so freed slots get reused and nothing ever shifts.
A double-ended queue (say "deck"): you can add and remove at both the front and the back, each in O(1).
A deque whose values stay in one order, like biggest to smallest, because you pop anything that would break it before adding a new item.

mentalModel.definition: A queue is a collection where items leave in the order they arrived (FIFO). enqueue adds at the back, dequeue removes from the front, and both run in O(1). A plain array makes dequeue cost O(n) because everyone shifts, so real queues track front and back instead. Most libraries use a circular array that grows when full (Java's ArrayDeque) or a deque built from fixed-size blocks (Python's collections.deque, and std::deque behind C++'s std::queue); a linked list works too (Java's LinkedList), but it is not the usual choice. A deque allows both ends, which also lets it serve as a stack.

useWhen: Things must be handled in the order they arrived: print jobs, tickets, requests, messages.
You explore a tree, grid or graph level by level, or the nearest things first (BFS): shortest path with equal steps, minimum moves.
Only the most recent items matter and old ones expire from the front: the last 3000 ms of calls, a moving average.
A window slides along and you need its maximum or minimum at every step: a monotonic deque.
notWhen: The newest item must come out first (undo, matching brackets, backtracking): that is a stack.
The best item must come out next, whatever order it arrived in (most urgent, smallest, top K): that is a heap.
You need an item by position or by value: an array or a hash map reaches it directly, a queue only shows its ends.

quiz.problem: Count how many requests arrived in the last 3000 milliseconds, every time a new request comes in. Timestamps only go up.
quiz.explanation: Time only moves forward, so the oldest request is always at the front. Enqueue each new one and dequeue from the front while it is older than 3000 ms.

quiz.problem: Given a binary tree, return its values level by level, from the root down, left to right.
quiz.explanation: Level by level is breadth-first search. It uses a queue inside, but the pattern to recognise is BFS: finish one level before starting the next.

quiz.problem: Check whether a string of brackets like ( [ { } ] ) is properly nested and closed.
quiz.explanation: The bracket you must close first is the one you opened last. Last in, first out is a stack, not a queue.

quiz.problem: An emergency room always treats the most critical patient next, no matter who arrived first.
quiz.explanation: A queue serves by arrival time. Serving by urgency needs a priority queue, which is a heap.

quiz.problem: Given an array and k, return the maximum of every window of k consecutive numbers, in O(n) time.
quiz.explanation: A heap works in O(n log n). A monotonic deque keeps only the candidates, biggest at the front, and each index enters and leaves once, so the whole pass is O(n).

pseudocode.text: buffer = 6 empty slots; front = 0, back = 5, size = 0
if size == 6: refuse (the line is full)
x = buffer[front], front = (front + 1) % 6, size = size - 1, return x

template.space: O(k) for a buffer of k slots
notes: Neither operation loops, so both are O(1). The only way to make dequeue slow is to shift items forward, which is exactly what front and back avoid.
front and back look the same when the line is full and when it is empty. Keep a size counter (as here), or leave one slot unused, to tell them apart.

Empty-queue behaviour depends on the language. Python's deque.popleft() raises IndexError, Java's Queue.poll() returns null (remove() throws NoSuchElementException), and C++'s std::queue::pop() on an empty queue is undefined behaviour, so check empty() first.

In real code use the library queue: collections.deque in Python (never list.pop(0), which shifts everything), ArrayDeque in Java, std::queue or std::deque in C++. They are mostly circular arrays or block lists, not plain linked lists.

For sliding window maximum the deque holds indexes, not values, so you can tell when the front has left the window. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, which is why the whole pass is O(n).

examples.title: Design Circular Queue
examples.problem: Build a queue with a fixed capacity k that reuses freed space. Support enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty and isFull, each in O(1).
examples.input: MyCircularQueue(3), enQueue(1), enQueue(2), enQueue(3), enQueue(4), Rear(), isFull(), deQueue(), enQueue(4), Rear()
examples.output: [null, true, true, true, false, 3, true, true, true, 4]
approach: Keep an array of k slots plus front, back and size. Start with front = 0 and back = k - 1 so the first enqueue lands in slot 0.
enQueue: if size == k return false. Otherwise back = (back + 1) % k, store the value there and grow size.
deQueue: if size == 0 return false. Otherwise front = (front + 1) % k and shrink size. The old value just stays unread.
In the example the fourth enQueue is refused (full), and after one deQueue the fifth lands in slot 0, so Rear() is 4.

examples.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
examples.problem: Build a first-in-first-out queue from two stacks. It must support push, pop, peek and empty.
examples.input: MyQueue(), push(1), push(2), peek(), pop(), empty()
approach: A stack hands back the newest item first, so pour one stack into another to reverse the order.
push always goes onto the inbox stack. Nothing else happens, so it is O(1).
pop and peek read from the outbox. Only when the outbox is empty, pour the whole inbox into it: the oldest item ends up on top.
Each item is poured at most once, so the cost per operation is O(1) amortized. After push(1), push(2) the first peek pours [1, 2] into [2, 1], and 1 comes out.

examples.title: Sliding Window Maximum
examples.problem: Given an array nums and a window size k, slide the window from the left end to the right end. Return the maximum of every window.
approach: Keep a deque of indexes whose values go from biggest at the front to smallest at the back. The front is always the window's maximum.
For each new index i, first pop the front if it has left the window (index i - k).
Then pop from the back while nums[back] < nums[i]: an older, smaller number can never be a maximum again. Push i at the back.
Once the first window is full (i >= k - 1), the front index gives that window's maximum. Every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so it is O(n).
examples.space: O(k) for the deque, plus the output

conceptQuiz.question: A circular queue has 6 slots and is not full. back is at slot 5. Where does the next enqueue go?
options: Slot 5 again, replacing the newest item
conceptQuiz.explanation: back moves to (5 + 1) % 6 = 0. The % wraps it round to the start, and slot 0 is free because the queue is not full.

conceptQuiz.question: Why does a circular queue not need to shift everyone forward after a dequeue?
options: Only front moves on; the items stay in their slots
It copies the line into a bigger array first
It sorts the slots after each dequeue
It stores the line as a linked list
conceptQuiz.explanation: The order lives in the two markers, not in the positions. Dequeue changes front by one and nothing else, so it costs O(1) however long the line is.

conceptQuiz.question: In a circular queue with 6 slots, front == (back + 1) % 6. Is the line full or empty?
options: Full, because a queue can never have 0 items
You can't tell from the markers alone, so keep a size counter
conceptQuiz.explanation: Both a full line and an empty one look like this. A size variable (or one deliberately unused slot) settles it.

conceptQuiz.question: You call dequeue on an empty queue. What happens?
options: It depends on the language: Python's deque.popleft() raises IndexError, Java's poll() returns null, C++'s pop() is undefined behaviour
It waits until someone enqueues, in every language
It always throws the same exception
conceptQuiz.explanation: Libraries disagree, so check for empty before you dequeue, or handle the language's own signal.

conceptQuiz.question: Sliding window maximum: the deque holds the values 9, 5, 4 from front to back, and a new number 7 arrives. What happens?
options: Pop 9 from the front, then push 7
Clear the deque and start again with 7
Pop 4 and 5 from the back, keep 9, push 7 at the back
Nothing: 7 is added at the front
conceptQuiz.explanation: 4 and 5 are older and smaller than 7, so they can never be a maximum again. 9 is bigger, so it stays in front, and 7 waits behind it as the next candidate.

practice.title: Number of Recent Calls
practice.insight: Timestamps only go up, so old pings sit at the front. Dequeue while the front is older than t - 3000; the queue's size is the answer.

practice.title: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
practice.insight: Simulate the line: whoever is served buys one ticket and rejoins the back if they still need more. Count seconds until person k is done.

practice.title: Implement Stack using Queues
practice.insight: After enqueueing x, rotate the older items behind it by moving size - 1 items from the front to the back, so the newest sits at the front.

practice.title: Design Circular Deque
practice.insight: Same circular buffer, but both ends move. Moving front backwards needs (front - 1 + k) % k so the index never goes negative.

practice.title: Reveal Cards In Increasing Order
practice.insight: Run the reveal rule on a queue of positions, not cards: the first position gets the smallest card, the next position goes to the back.

practice.title: Rotting Oranges
practice.insight: Queue every rotten orange first. Each round rots the neighbours of everything currently in the queue, so the number of rounds is the answer.

practice.title: Longest Continuous Subarray With Absolute Diff Less Than or Equal to Limit
practice.insight: Keep one monotonic deque for the window's max and one for its min. Shrink from the left while max minus min is over the limit.

practice.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
practice.insight: Work on prefix sums, with negatives allowed. A deque of indexes with increasing prefix sums lets you pop the front when it is long enough and the back when it can't help.

overview: Explain why a queue serves items in first-in, first-out order.
Trace enqueue and dequeue on a circular buffer with wrap-around.
Explain why moving only front and back keeps each step O(1).
Use a monotonic deque to track a sliding window's maximum.
Choose a stack instead when the newest item must come out first.
